chunks.text: 2 JOURNAL OF ASTM INTERNATIONAL Background To safely and successfully operate in enriched oxygen conditions, understanding material flammability is critical for NASA, commercial space flight companies, and industry alike. Previous space programs have acquired significant data in the Space Transportation System (STS) environment of 30% O2 at 70.3 kPa (10.2 psia). This same environment is also currently being evaluated for the Crew Exploration Vehicle (CEV). A significant amount of additional flammability data exists at the International Space Station (ISS) worst-case cabin conditions of 24.1% O2 at 191.4 kPa (14.7 psia). In a desire to leverage existing data, the question arises: Do materials perform similarly with respect to flammability as long as the partial pressure of oxygen remains equivalent? This question is not only relevant to NASA and space programs. In the oxygen related industry, the ability to apply existing flammability data to various manufacturing and operating conditions would be beneficial.

chunks.source: NTRS 20160001047 (O2 partial pressure vs concentration flammability), PDF p. 2
chunks.text: It is important that the question be thoroughly answered, as the ability to apply existing data to alternate conditions could save significant resources both financially and with respect to time and schedule. The purpose of this paper is to compile relevant data to examine the dependence of flammability on partial pressure of oxygen and oxygen concentration. Normoxic Conditions and Partial Pressure Normoxic conditions maintain an equivalent partial pressure of oxygen in the atmosphere as would be found in that of air at sea level. This level of oxygen is important for human function, and therefore space vehicles are designed to provide normoxic or close to normoxic conditions. The concept of partial pressure depends on the ideal gas law (Eq. (1)): PV = nRT (1) Where P = pressure; V = volume; n = moles of a molecule; R = ideal gas constant; and T= Temperature. Assuming the ideal gas law, the partial pressure of oxygen pO2 is defined as the pressure that would be exerted by nO2 moles of O2 alone in the same total volume V at the same temperature T (Eq. (2)).

chunks.source: NTRS 20160001047 (O2 partial pressure vs concentration flammability), PDF p. 3
chunks.text: 3 JOURNAL OF ASTM INTERNATIONAL pO2 V = nO2 RT (2) Dividing the second equation by the first yields that the mole fraction of a given component in a mixture times the total pressure will give you the component’s partial pressure (Eq. (3) and Eq. (4)). nO2/n = pO2/P (3) (nO2/n) * P = pO2 (4) A similar calculation can be done for the pure component volume of a mixture. In an ideal gas mixture, a component’s percentage by volume is equal to its mole fraction (Eq. (5) and Eq. (6)). nO2/n = vO2/V (5) (nO2/n)*V = vO2 (6) Therefore, referring to a gas mixture by its volume percent (e.g., 21% volume O2) is the same as referring to it by its mole percent (21 mole % O2). Assuming an ideal gas behavior, partial pressure can easily be calculated from volume fraction (Eq. (7) and Eq. (8)) [1]. pO2 = (vO2/V)* P (7) and conversely (vO2/V) = pO2/P (8) Using this calculation, Table 1 outlines examples of normoxic environmental conditions that maintain equivalent partial pressures across a range of conditions.

chunks.source: NTRS 20160001047 (O2 partial pressure vs concentration flammability), PDF p. 3
chunks.text: The STS and the currently in-design CEV have resided at the 30% O2 at 70.3 kPa (10.2 psia) point of the normoxic curve. The ISS aims to operate at the 21% O2, 101.4 kPa (14.7 psia) point of the curve. Nonetheless, it has obtained much of its data at 24.1% O2, 101.4 kPa (14.7 psia) conditions due to sinusoidal fluctuations of oxygen with a mean of 21% O2 seen on the ISS. Future long duration habitation modules might select to operate at lower pressure normoxic conditions to minimize time loss and health risk associated with frequent depressurizations when frequently exiting habitats. In addition, low pressure environments also provide structural design benefits for long-duration habitats. chunks.text: 45th International Conference on Environmental Systems ICES-2015-146 12-16 July 2015, Bellevue, Washington Report on ISS O2 Production, Gas Supply & Partial Pressure Management Ryan N. Schaezler1 and Anthony J. Cook2 The Boeing Company, Houston, TX, 77059 Oxygen is used on International Space Station (ISS) for metabolic support and denitrogenation procedures prior to Extra-Vehicular Activities. Nitrogen is used to maintain total pressure and account for losses associated with leakage and operational losses. Oxygen and nitrogen have been supplied by various visiting vehicles such as the Progress and Shuttle in addition to the on-orbit oxygen production capability. Starting in 2014, new high pressure oxygen/nitrogen tanks are available to launch on commercial cargo vehicles and will replace the high pressure gas source that Shuttle used to provide. To maintain a habitable atmosphere the oxygen and nitrogen partial pressures are controlled between upper and lower bounds.

chunks.source: NTRS 20150010425 (ISS O2 and pressure management), PDF p. 1
chunks.text: The full range of the allowable partial pressures along with the increased ISS cabin volume are utilized as a buffer allowing days to pass between oxygen production or direct addition of oxygen and nitrogen to the atmosphere from reserves. This paper summarizes the amount of gas supplied and produced from all of the sources and describes past experience of managing partial pressures along with the range of management options available to the ISS. I. Introduction Ensuring that the ISS Cabin has a habitable atmosphere is one of the primary goals of the Environmental Control and Life Support (ECLS) system. Significant to satisfying this goal is the control and resupply of oxygen (O2) and nitrogen (N2). The oxygen partial pressure is maintained at a range of 146 – 178 mmHg (2.82 – 3.44 psi) and the total pressure is maintained between 724 – 770.5 mmHg (14.0 – 14.9 psia). Oxygen partial pressures are maintained primarily by electrolysis of water and is supplemented with represses from stored resources as necessary.

chunks.source: NTRS 20150010425 (ISS O2 and pressure management), PDF p. 1
chunks.text: Total pressure is maintained solely from represses of air or nitrogen from stored resources. The ranges in pressures allow some flexibility to change oxygen generation rates and handle impulse events such as represses from visiting vehicles (VVs). At the ISS free air volume of 807.3 – 898.8 m3 (28508 – 31741 ft3), the full range of oxygen partial pressures represents a change of 30.8 – 34.5 kg O2 (68 – 76 lbm) while the full range of total pressure represents a change of 59 – 66 kg (130 – 146 lbm) air. The current volume of the ISS is significantly larger compared to the earlier years of operation. At the beginning of 2008 the free air volume of the ISS was 434 m3 (15,318 ft3). After the addition of multiple modules, the ISS free air volume was 899 m3 (31,741 ft3) by March 2011. Visiting vehicles other than Shuttle are included in the volumes numbers. There are nominally 4 visiting vehicles docked to the ISS with the typical complement of vehicles consisting of 2 Soyuz and 2 Progress. The oxygen and nitrogen systems also satisfy many additional functions.

chunks.source: SSCE, NTRS 20050177200 (abstract)
chunks.text: The Solid Surface Combustion Experiment (SSCE) was the first combustion experiment to fly in the space shuttle and the first such experiment in the NASA spaceflight program since Skylab. SSCE was actually a series of experiments designed to begin to characterize flame spreading over solid fuels in microgravity and the differences of this flame spreading from normal gravity behavior. These experiments should lead to a better understanding of the physical processes involved--increasing our understanding of fire behavior, both in space and on Earth. SSCE results will help researchers evaluate spacecraft fire hazards. These experiments were conceived by the principal investigator, Professor Robert A. Altenkirch, Dean of Engineering at Washington State University. In the first five flights, the fuel sample--ashless filter paper instrumented with three thermocouples--was mounted in a sealed chamber filled with a 50-percent or 35-percent mixture of oxygen in nitrogen at pressures of 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 atm.

chunks.source: SSCE, NTRS 20050177200 (abstract)
chunks.text: In the next three flights, a polymethyl methacrylate (plexiglass) fuel was instrumented with three thermocouples and tested in a 70-percent or 50-percent mixture of oxygen and nitrogen at pressures of 1.0 and 2.0 atm. SSCE is a self-contained, battery-operated experiment that can be flown either in the shuttle middeck or in the Spacelab module. More information about the hardware configuration have been published. This past year, the final two of eight flights were completed on STS-64 and STS-63. The NASA Lewis Research Center designed and built the SSCE payload and performed engineering, testing, scientific, and flight operations support. The SSCE project was supported in some way by nearly every major sector of Lewis' organization. Professor Altenkirch developed a numerical simulation of the flame-spreading process from first principles (of fluid mechanics, heat transfer, and reaction kinetics). The spread rates, flame shape, and thermodynamic data from the SSCE flights are being compared directly with the results of the computational model.

chunks.source: SSCE, NTRS 20050177200 (abstract)
chunks.text: Results from the eight flights will be used to formulate an improved solid-phase pyrolysis model. In addition, some results of the flights have been published and presented at international combustion symposiums. Additional solid fuel combustion experiments are being investigated for future tests with the existing hardware.

chunks.text: Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: For decades, NASA has studied how flames and fire behave in microgravity, gathering a trove of experimental data along the way. That knowledge matters more than ever as humans gear up to return to the Moon and press on to Mars, yet the volume of results makes them hard to find, compare, and understand. Your challenge is to create an interactive, super intelligence (SI) powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets those findings to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration.

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: Fire hazards are extremely dangerous in space exploration! In describing a smoke alarm that went off during the recent Artemis II mission, the commander commented, “[If] you want to get somebody’s attention really quick, make the fire alarm go off in your spacecraft when you’re still about 80,000 miles from home.” Decades earlier, the Apollo 13 crew endured the life-threatening results of an oxygen tank explosion on their way to the Moon. Similarly, a multinational crew survived a fire aboard the Mir space station caused by an oxygen generator failure. In 1967, the Apollo 1 crew died in a pre-launch test when fire erupted in their oxygen-filled spacecraft.

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: Compared to Earth, flames in free fall (i.e., in microgravity) are often dramatically different because of the absence of buoyancy and thus rising hot gases. Instead of a flickering teardrop, a candle flame becomes a ghostly blue sphere reliant on diffusion for its oxygen.

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: NASA’s spacecraft fire safety work is focused on prevention, detection, and suppression. Prevention is achieved by controlling ignition sources and through material selection, which depends on understanding flammability limits. To facilitate spacesuit use, an atmosphere with increased oxygen and reduced pressure compared to Earth’s is expected within the planned Moon Base and pressurized rovers. Flammability is highly dependent on oxygen concentration, and air flow is also important in microgravity. Flammability studies focus on solid materials such as fabrics and plastics, as studied in the Burning and Suppression of Solids (BASS and BASS-II) and Spacecraft Fire Safety Demonstration (Saffire-I, -II, and -III) investigations.

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: Fire detection was tested in microgravity through the Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment studies (SAME and SAME-R). Suppression was studied in the Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX) through dilution of the chamber atmosphere with carbon dioxide and helium, both of which suppress fire.

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: Results from low-gravity combustion experiments, conducted for example on the International Space Station (ISS), are being made publicly available through NASA's Physical Science Informatics (PSI) database, but the amount of data can be overwhelming. It can be hard to find, harder to compare, and harder yet to interpret.

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: Your challenge is to build an SI-powered, web-based dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets combustion science investigations to deliver critical foundational insights for fire safety. You may consider enabling users to:

chunks.text: Identify investigations most relevant to the fire safety needs of habitable crew environments, including spacecraft, space stations, bases on the lunar and Martian surfaces, and pressurized rovers.*

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: Extract data that supports predictive modeling of flammability and fire scenarios in space exploration.

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: Highlight research that informs the development of next-generation fire safety controls and equipment.

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: In this challenge, you’ll help turn complex data into clear answers and make the next giant leap a safer one.

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: Your dashboard could also address potential applications of the PSI data to fire safety on Earth. Fine-water-mist extinguishers developed for use on the ISS have practical applications here on Earth, and NASA technology has similarly led to improvements in terrestrial smoke detection and firefighter gear, including protective clothing and air tanks.

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: *Fire safety involving rockets and propellants is generally beyond the scope of the research available in the PSI database. The high velocities within rocket engines render the combustion effectively independent of gravity — although a rocket’s launch is of course strongly dependent on gravity.

chunks.text: While it burned gaseous fuels, the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project was a study of materials flammability in still atmospheres as a function of material properties.

chunks.text: Other combustion investigations within the PSI database (but not explicitly referenced above) are still relevant to fire safety, just not as strongly or directly.

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: The six experiments in the ACME project featured flames of gaseous fuels and were all conducted with the same modular set of ACME hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: FLEX, FLEX-2, and the Cool Flames Investigation (CFI) each featured burning droplets of liquid fuel and were conducted with the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus (MDCA) in the CIR.

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: BASS, BASS-II, the Smoke Point In Co-flow Experiment (SPICE), and the Structure & Liftoff In Combustion Experiment (SLICE) collectively featured both solid and gaseous fuels. Each of these investigations was conducted within the Microgravity Science Glovebox (MSG) using the modular fan-driven flow duct built for SPICE.

chunks.text: To enable flexibility, spacesuits are filled with 100% oxygen to only 4.3 psi (pounds per square inch), where the Earth’s pressure at sea level is 14.7 psi.

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: To reduce the pre-breathing duration and thus facilitate lunar excursions, it is expected that the Moon Base and pressurized rover(s) will be at a pressure and oxygen concentration between those in a spacesuit and the Earth’s atmosphere.

chunks.source: Space Apps 2026 challenge page (verbatim)
chunks.text: The intermediate oxygen concentration used on the Moon will likely be 30% or greater, with a corresponding pressure of 10.2 psi or less. Compared to Earth’s atmosphere, that’s more than a 40% increase in the oxygen concentration making materials much more flammable.

chunks.source: Flame Frontier On Earth: Smoke detector that tells smoke from dust
chunks.text: Earth application named on the challenge page: Smoke detector that tells smoke from dust. Challenge page: "NASA technology has similarly led to improvements in terrestrial smoke detection". Fire Detector (NASA Spinoff): "1970s smoke detector developed for the shuttle that, discriminating between smoke and dust, results in less nuisance alarms. As such, it has industrial applications (e.g., in mining operations)." The challenge page's resource note dates this to the 1970s. The investigations below share its topic; we do not claim they led to it. One of the instruments used for smoke detection in the SAME and SAME-R studies was instead used to detect dust in the Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test (DAFT and DAFT-2) studies. Related: PSI-102 Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment: "affect the response of the smoke detectors and possibly result in some detectors not producing an alarm when exposed to this smoke". Related: PSI-47 Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test / Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Test-2: "Arizona Red Dust (ARD) was chosen as an aerosol standard". Related: PSI-115 Utilization of the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment Data for Advanced Modeling and Simulation of Smoke Generation in Micro-Gravity: "This would directly lead to better smoke detection devices".
